entities.summary:
Macías, often referred to as Macías O Namorado (the Enamored), was a seminal Galician troubadour and one of the last exponents of the Galician-Portuguese lyric tradition, whose life and work are shrouded in romantic legend and historical ambiguity. Flourishing at the close of the 14th century, his death is traditionally placed around 1401. He represents a poignant bridge between the golden age of medieval Iberian courtly love poetry and its eventual decline, embodying the ideals of courtly love, known as *amor cortés*, in a period of shifting cultural and political landscapes within the nascent kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula. His poetic legacy, though small in corpus, significantly influenced later Spanish and Portuguese lyricists, cementing his place as an enduring figure in the literary imagination of Southern Europe.

Details of Macías's life are scarce, primarily derived from later literary accounts and inferences from his surviving poems. He is believed to have been a knight in the service of Fernán Pérez de Andrade, "O Bo" (the Good), a powerful Galician nobleman and military figure. The central narrative surrounding Macías revolves around his intense, unrequited love for a noblewoman, often identified as the wife of a rival lord or even his own patron. This passionate devotion, expressed in his *cantigas de amor* (songs of love), reportedly led to his imprisonment and eventual death, possibly by a jealous husband or a disillusioned patron, though the precise circumstances remain debated. His poetic output consists of a handful of *cantigas*, characterized by their profound emotional intensity, intricate metaphorical language, and adherence to the conventions of courtly love, making him a paradigm of the suffering lover.

entities.summary:
Macías was a Galician troubadour and one of the last Galician medieval poets.
He was born in 1401 in Galicia, Spain, to a noble family and began his poetic career at a young age, drawing inspiration from the works of earlier Galician poets such as Martín Codax and Pero López de Rueda. His poetry is characterized by its use of the galician-portuguese language and its exploration of themes related to love, nature, and social justice.
Macías' work had a lasting impact on the development of Galician literature, influencing generations of poets and writers who followed in his footsteps. He died in 1401, at the age of 0, leaving behind a body of work that is still studied and admired today for its beauty, depth, and historical significance.
Macías' legacy can be seen in the many festivals and celebrations held in Galicia every year to honor his memory and celebrate the rich cultural heritage of the region.
